\label{thm:main theorem}
The consensus time of 3-Majority is $\widetilde{\Theta}(\min\{\sqrt{n},k\})$\footnote{$\widetilde{\Theta}(\cdot)$ and $\widetilde O(\cdot)$ hide polylogarithmic factors.} with high probability\footnote{The term ``with high probability'' means that the event holds with probability $1-O(n^{-c})$ for some constant $c>0$.} for all $2\le k\le n$.
Moreover, if $k = o(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ and the most popular opinion is supported by $\omega(\sqrt{n\log n})$ more vertices than any other opinion, then 3-Majority reaches consensus on the most popular opinion with high probability.

Similarly, the consensus time of 2-Choices is $\tilde{\Theta}(k)$ with high probability for all $2\le k \le n$. Moreover, if $k=o(n/(\log n)^2)$ and 
the most popular opinion is supported by $\omega(\sqrt{\alpha_1 n\log n})$ more vertices than any other opinion where $\alpha_1$ is the fraction of vertices supporting the most popular opinion, then 2-Choices reaches consensus on the most popular opinion.

nodes.statement: Combining crefthm:consensus time large alphanorm,thm:growth of alphanorm, we immediately obtain the following upper bounds that hold for any initial configuration. nodes.statement: Let n,kin N be such that 1le kle n. The 3-Majority (or 2-Choices) is a discrete-time Markov chain (opn_t)_tinN_0 over the state space [k]^V for a finite set V with |V|=n, where (opn_t)_tinN_0 is defined as follows: In 3-Majority, for every tge 1, opn_tin[k]^V is obtained from opn_t-1in[k]^V by the following procedure: item For each vertex vin V, select uniformly random w_1,w_2,w_3in V, independent and with replacement. item Define opn_t(v)in [k] by \[ opn_t(v) = opn_t-1(w_1) & if opn_t-1(w_1)=opn_t-1(w_2), \\ opn_t-1(w_3) & otherwise. \] In 2-Choices, for every tge 1, opn_tin[k]^V is obtained from opn_t-1in[k]^V by the following procedure: item For each vertex vin V, select uniformly random w_1,w_2in V, independently and with replacement. item Define opn_t(v)in [k] by \[ opn_t(v) = opn_t-1(w_1) & if opn_t-1(w_1)=opn_t-1(w_2), \\ opn_t-1(v) & otherwise. \] For both dynamics, the consensus time tau_cons is the stopping time defined by \[ tau_cons = infcbra*tgeq 0 colon for some iin[k] and all vin V, opn_t(v)=i. \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:3-Majority and 2-Choices}
  Let $n,k\in \mathbb{N}$ be such that $1\le k\le n$.
  The \emph{3-Majority} (or \emph{2-Choices}) 
  is a discrete-time Markov chain $(\mathsf{opn}_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ over the state space $[k]^V$ for a finite set $V$ with $|V|=n$, where $(\mathsf{opn}_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is defined as follows:

  In 3-Majority, for every $t\ge 1$, $\mathsf{opn}_t\in[k]^V$ is obtained from $\mathsf{opn}_{t-1}\in[k]^V$ by the following procedure:
  \begin{enumerate}
      \item For each vertex $v\in V$, select uniformly random $w_1,w_2,w_3\in V$, independent and with replacement.
      \item Define $\mathsf{opn}_{t}(v)\in [k]$ by
      \[
          \mathsf{opn}_t(v) = 
          \begin{cases}
              \mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(w_1) & \text{if $\mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(w_1)=\mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(w_2)$}, \\
              \mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(w_3) & \text{otherwise}.
          \end{cases}
      \]
  \end{enumerate}
  
  In 2-Choices, for every $t\ge 1$, $\mathsf{opn}_t\in[k]^V$ is obtained from $\mathsf{opn}_{t-1}\in[k]^V$ by the following procedure:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For each vertex $v\in V$, select uniformly random $w_1,w_2\in V$, independently and with replacement.
        \item Define $\mathsf{opn}_{t}(v)\in [k]$ by
        \[
            \mathsf{opn}_t(v) = 
            \begin{cases}
                \mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(w_1) & \text{if $\mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(w_1)=\mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(w_2)$}, \\
                \mathsf{opn}_{t-1}(v) & \text{otherwise}.
            \end{cases}
        \]
    \end{enumerate}

  For both dynamics, the \emph{consensus time} $\tau_{\mathrm{cons}}$ is the stopping time defined by
  \[
      \tau_{\mathrm{cons}} = \inf\cbra*{t\geq 0 \colon \text{for some $i\in[k]$ and all $v\in V$, $\mathsf{opn}_t(v)=i$}}.
  \]

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:basic quantities}
    Let $(\mathsf{opn}_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$ be 3-Majority or 2-Choices.
    We define the following quantities.
\begin{enumerate}
  
    \item  The \emph{fractional population} is the sequence of random vectors $(\alpha_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ where each $\alpha_t\in[0,1]^k$ is defined by
  \[
      \alpha_t(i) = \frac{\abs*{\{v\in V\colon \mathsf{opn}_t(v)=i\}}}{n}.
  \]

  \item For $t\ge 0$ and $i,j\in[k]$, the \emph{bias} $\delta_t(i,j)$ is defined as $\delta_t(i,j) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \alpha_t(i) - \alpha_t(j)$. If opinions $i,j$ are clear from context, we use the abbreviated notation $\delta_t=\delta_t(i,j)$.
  \item Let $\gamma_t=\norm{\alpha_t}^2_2=\sum_{i\in [k]}\alpha_t(i)^2$ denote the squared $\ell^2$-norm of $\alpha_t$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Consider lambdain R such that abslambda D<3. For such lambda, we have abslambda Xleq abslambdaabsXleq abslambda D<3. Hence, applying creflem:Bernstein lemma to lambda X, Eqty[e^lambda X] &leq Eqty[1+lambda X+fraclambda^2X^2/21-abslambda X/3] &&(creflem:Bernstein lemma)\\ &leq 1+Eqty[fraclambda^2X^2/21-(abslambda D)/3] &&(because E[X]=0)\\ &leq expqty(fraclambda^2E[X^2]/21-(abslambda D)/3) &&(because 1+xleq e^x)\\ &= expqty(fraclambda^2Var[X]/21-(abslambda D)/3) &&(because Var[X]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2=E[X^2]) and we obtain the claim.

Consider $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\abs{\lambda} D<3$.
    For such $\lambda$, we have $\abs{\lambda X}\leq \abs{\lambda}\abs{X}\leq \abs{\lambda} D<3$.
    Hence, applying \cref{lem:Bernstein lemma} to $\lambda X$, 
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\qty[\mathrm{e}^{\lambda X}]
    &\leq \mathbb{E}\qty[1+\lambda X+\frac{\lambda^2X^2/2}{1-\abs{\lambda X}/3}] &&(\textrm{\cref{lem:Bernstein lemma}})\\
    &\leq 1+\mathbb{E}\qty[\frac{\lambda^2X^2/2}{1-(\abs{\lambda} D)/3}] &&(\textrm{$\because$ $\mathbb{E}[X]=0$})\\
    &\leq \exp\qty(\frac{\lambda^2\mathbb{E}[X^2]/2}{1-(\abs{\lambda} D)/3}) &&(\textrm{$\because$ $1+x\leq \mathrm{e}^x$})\\
    &= \exp\qty(\frac{\lambda^2\mathbf{Var}[X]/2}{1-(\abs{\lambda} D)/3}) &&(\textrm{$\because$ $\mathbf{Var}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2=\mathbb{E}[X^2]$})
    
    \end{align*}
    and we obtain the claim.

\label{lem:Freedman stopping time additive}
 Let $(X_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$ be a sequence of random variables and
 let $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be a filtration such that $ X_t $ is $ \mathcal{F}_t $-measurable for all $t\ge 0$.
 Let $\tau$ be a stopping time with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$.
 Let $D,s \ge 0$ and $R\in\mathbb{R}$ be parameters.
 Suppose the following condition holds for any $t\geq 1$: conditioned on $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$, 
      \begin{enumerate}[label=$(C\arabic*)$]
        \item $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\rbra*{\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[X_t]-X_{t-1}-R}\leq 0$, \label{item:C1}
        \item $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\rbra*{X_t-X_{t-1}-R}$ satisfies one-sided $\qty(D,s)$-Bernstein condition. \label{item:C2}
      \end{enumerate}
    For a parameter $h>0$, define stopping times
    \begin{align*} 
      &\tau_X^+\mathrel{\mathop:}= \inf\qty{t\geq 0\colon X_t\geq X_0+h}, \\
      &\tau_X^- \mathrel{\mathop:}= \inf\qty{t\geq 0\colon X_t\leq X_0-h}.
    \end{align*}
    Then, we have the following:
      \begin{enumerate}
        
        \item \label{item:positive drift} Suppose $R\geq 0$. Then, for any $h,T>0$ such that $z \mathrel{\mathop:}= h-R\cdot T > 0$, we have
        \[
        \Pr\qty[\tau_X^+ \le \min\{T,\tau\}] 
         \le \exp\qty(- \frac{z^2/2}{s T + (z D)/3}).
        \]
        \item \label{item:negative drift} Suppose $R< 0$. Then, for any $h,T>0$ such that $ z \mathrel{\mathop:}= (-R)\cdot T - h > 0$, we have
        \[
        \Pr\qty[\min\cbra{\tau_X^-,\tau} >T] 
         \le \exp\qty(- \frac{z^2/2}{s T + (z D)/3}).
        \]
      \end{enumerate}

\label{lem:BC for SP}
      Let $(X_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$ be a sequence of random variables and
      let $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be a filtration such that $ X_t $ is $ \mathcal{F}_t $-measurable for all $t\ge 0$.
      Let $(D_{t})_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$ and $(s_{t})_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$ are $ \mathcal{F}_t $-measurable random variables.
      Let $\tau$ be a stopping time with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$.
      Suppose that $X_t$ conditioned on $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$ satisfies $(D_{t-1},s_{t-1})$-Bernstein condition, $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1} D_{t-1}\leq D$, and $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1} s_{t-1}\leq s$ for some non-negative parameters $D$ and $s$.
      Then, 
      both $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}X_t$ and $-\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}X_t$ conditioned on $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$ satisfy $(D,s)$-Bernstein condition.

nodes.statement: Consider the quantities defined in crefdef:basic quantities for 3-Majority or 2-Choices. Fix two distinct opinions i,jin [k]. item For constants c_alpha^uparrow,c_alpha^downarrow>0, define &tau^uparrow_i = infcbra* t ge 0 colon alpha_t(i) ge (1+c_alpha^uparrow)alpha_0(i),\\ &tau^downarrow_i = infcbra* t ge 0 colon alpha_t(i) le (1-c_alpha^downarrow)alpha_0(i). item For constants c^uparrow_delta,c^downarrow_delta >0 and a parameter x_delta = x_delta(n) in [1/n, 1], define &tau^uparrow_delta = infcbra* t ge 0 colon delta_t(i,j) ge (1+c^uparrow_delta) delta_0(i,j) ,\\ &tau^downarrow_delta = infcbra* t ge 0 colon delta_t(i,j) le (1-c^downarrow_delta) delta_0(i,j) , \\ &tau^+_delta= infqtytgeq 0: absdelta_t(i,j)geq x_delta. item For constants c^uparrow_gamma,c^downarrow_gamma>0 and a parameter x_gamma = x_gamma(n)in[0,1], define &tau^uparrow_gamma = inf\tgeq 0: gamma_tgeq (1+c^uparrow_gamma)gamma_0\, \\ &tau^downarrow_gamma = infcbra*tgeq 0: gamma_tleq (1-c^downarrow_gamma)gamma_0, \\ &tau^+_gamma mathrelmathop:= infqtytgeq 0: gamma_tgeq x_gamma. item For a constant 0le c^weak<1/2, we say that an opinion iin[k] is weak at round t if alpha_t(i) le (1-c^weak) gamma_t. We define &tau^weak_i = infcbra* t ge 0 colon alpha_t(i) le (1-c^weak) gamma_t . item For a constant c^active>0 satisfying c^downarrow_gamma<c^active<c^weak, we say that an opinion i in [k] is active at round t if alpha_t(i) ge (1-c^active)cdot gamma_0. We define tau^active_i = infqty t ge 0 colon alpha_t(i) ge (1-c^active)cdot gamma_0 . The constants c_alpha^uparrow,c_alpha^downarrow,c^uparrow_delta,c^downarrow_delta,c^uparrow_gamma,c^downarrow_gamma,c^weak,c^active are universal constants, e.g., we can set c^uparrow_alpha=c^downarrow_alpha=c^weak=1/10, c^uparrow_delta=c^downarrow_delta=c^active=1/20, and c^uparrow_gamma=c^downarrow_gamma=1/30 for both 3-Majority and 2-Choices.

We define &tau^weak_i = infcbra* t ge 0 colon alpha_t(i) le (1-c^weak) gamma_t . item For a constant c^active>0 satisfying c^downarrow_gamma<c^active<c^weak, we say that an opinion i in [k] is active at round t if alpha_t(i) ge (1-c^active)cdot gamma_0. We define tau^active_i = infqty t ge 0 colon alpha_t(i) ge (1-c^active)cdot gamma_0 . nodes.name: Summary of the drift terms of alpha_t, delta_t, and gamma_t used in creflem:drift analysis for basic
nodes.statement: |c|c| hline Drift & Condition of t \\ hline hline E_t-1[alpha_t(i)-alpha_t-1(i)]leq Calpha_0(i)^2 & t-1<tau^uparrow_i \\ hline E_t-1[alpha_t(i)-alpha_t-1(i)]geq - Calpha_0(i)^2 & t-1<min\tau^weak_i,tau^uparrow_i\ \\ hline E_t-1[alpha_t(i)-alpha_t-1(i)]leq 0 &t-1<min\tau^active_i,tau^downarrow_gamma\ \\ hline hline E_t-1[delta_t(i,j)-delta_t-1(i,j)]geq 0 & t-1<min\tau^weak_j,tau^downarrow_delta\ \\ hline E_t-1[delta_t(i,j)-delta_t-1(i,j)]geq Calpha_0(i)delta_0(i,j) & t-1<min\tau^weak_j,tau^downarrow_delta,tau^downarrow_i\ \\ hline hline E_t-1[gamma_t-gamma_t-1]geq 0 & forall t \\ hline captionSummary of the drift terms of alpha_t, delta_t, and gamma_t used in creflem:drift analysis for basic (for both 3-Majority and 2-Choices). For each item, C>0 is a carefully chosen constant.
nodes.raw_latex:
\centering
  \begin{tabular}{|c|c|}
  \hline
  Drift & Condition of $t$  \\ \hline \hline
  $\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i)]\leq C\alpha_0(i)^2$ & $t-1<\tau^{\uparrow}_i$  \\ \hline 
  $\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i)]\geq - C\alpha_0(i)^2$ & $t-1<\min\{\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_i,\tau^{\uparrow}_i\}$   \\ \hline
  $\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i)]\leq 0$ &$t-1<\min\{\tau^{\mathrm{active}}_i,\tau^{\downarrow}_\gamma\}$   \\ \hline \hline
  $\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\delta_t(i,j)-\delta_{t-1}(i,j)]\geq 0$ & $t-1<\min\{\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_j,\tau^{\downarrow}_\delta\}$   \\ \hline
  $\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\delta_t(i,j)-\delta_{t-1}(i,j)]\geq C\alpha_{0}(i)\delta_{0}(i,j)$ & $t-1<\min\{\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_j,\tau^{\downarrow}_\delta,\tau^{\downarrow}_i\}$   \\ \hline \hline
  $\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\gamma_t-\gamma_{t-1}]\geq 0$ & $\forall t$  \\ \hline 
  \end{tabular}
  \caption{Summary of the drift terms of $\alpha_t, \delta_t$, and $\gamma_t$ used in \cref{lem:drift analysis for basic} (for both 3-Majority and 2-Choices).
  For each item, $C>0$ is a carefully chosen constant.}
  \label{table:drift}

nodes.name: Drift analysis for basic quantities
nodes.statement: Consider stopping times defined in crefdef:stopping times. Fix two distinct opinions i,jin [k]. Then, we have the following: item For any constant varepsilonin (0,1), let C_mboxtiny()mathrelmathop:= frac (1 - varepsilon) c_alpha^uparrow (1+c_alpha^uparrow)^2. Then, we have Prqty[ tau^uparrow_i le fracC_mboxtiny() alpha_0(i) ] le expqty(-Omegaqty( nalpha_0(i)^2 )) & for 3-Majority,\\[10pt] expqty( -Omegaqty( nalpha_0(i) ) ) & for 2-Choices. item For any constant varepsilon in (0,1), let C_mboxtiny()mathrelmathop:= frac(1-c^weak)(1-varepsilon)c^downarrow_alphac^weak (1+c_alpha^uparrow)^2. Then, we have Prqty[ tau^downarrow_i le mincbra*tau^weak_i,tau^uparrow_i,fracC_mboxtiny()alpha_0(i) ] le expqty(-Omegaqty( nalpha_0(i)^2 )) & for 3-Majority,\\[10pt] expqty( -Omegaqty( nalpha_0(i) ) ) & for 2-Choices. item For any T>0, we have Prqty[tau^active_ileq min\T,tau^downarrow_gamma\] leq expqty(-Omegaqty(fracngamma_0T)) & for 3-Majority, \\[10pt] expqty(-Omegaqty(fracngamma_0Tgamma_0+1)) & for 2-Choices. item For any T> 0, we have Prqty[ tau^downarrow_delta le min\tau^weak_j,tau^uparrow_i,T\ ] le expqty( -Omegaqty( fracndelta_0(i,j)^2alpha_0(i)T+delta_0(i,j) ) ) & for 3-Majority, \\[10pt] expqty( -Omegaqty(fracn delta_0(i,j)^2alpha_0(i)^2 T+delta_0(i,j)) ) & for 2-Choices. item For any constant varepsilonin (0,1), let C_mboxtiny()mathrelmathop:= frac(1-c^weak)(1+varepsilon)c^uparrow_delta(1-2c^weak)(1-c^downarrow_alpha)(1-c^downarrow_delta). Then, we have Prqty[ mincbra* tau^uparrow_delta, tau^weak_j, tau^downarrow_delta, tau^uparrow_i, tau^downarrow_i > fracC_mboxtiny()alpha_0(i)] leq expqty(-Omega(ndelta_0(i,j)^2)) & for 3-Majority, \\[10pt] expqty(-Omegaqty(fracndelta_0(i,j)^2alpha_0(i))) & for 2-Choices. item For any T>0, we have Prqty[tau^downarrow_gammaleq mincbra*T,tau^uparrow_gamma]le expqty(-Omegaqty(fracnsqrtgamma_0T)) & for 3-Majority, \\[10pt] expqty(-Omegaqty(fracnT+gamma_0^-1/2)) & for 2-Choices.

Let $X_t=\alpha_t(i)$, $\tau=\tau^{\uparrow}_i$, and $R = 
        (1+c_\alpha^{\uparrow})^2\alpha_0(i)^2$.
    Suppose $\tau>t-1$.
    For both 2-Choices and 3-Majority, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_{t-1}\sbra{\alpha_t(i)}
    =\alpha_{t-1}(i)\qty(1+\alpha_{t-1}(i)-\gamma_{t-1})
    \leq \alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(i)^2
    \leq \alpha_{t-1}(i)+R.
    \end{align*}
    Therefore, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[X_t]-X_{t-1}-R)
    =\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\alpha_t(i)]-\alpha_{t-1}(i)-R)
    \leq 0.
    \end{align*}
    That is, we checked the condition \ref{item:C1} of \cref{lem:Freedman stopping time additive}.


    Now we check that 3-Majority and 2-Choices satisfy \ref{item:C2} or \ref{item:C2'} for $D = \frac{1}{n}$ and
        \begin{align} 
       s = \begin{cases}
        O\qty( \frac{\alpha_0(i)}{n} )	& \text{ for 3-Majority},\\[10pt]
        O\qty( \frac{\alpha_0(i)^2}{n} ) & \text{ for 2-Choices}.
       \end{cases} \label{eq:variance tauiup}
    \end{align}

    \paragraph*{3-Majority.}
    We have $\alpha_{t-1}(i) \le (1+c_\alpha^{\uparrow})\alpha_0(i)$ if $ t-1 < \tau $.
    Hence, from \cref{lem:BC for SP} and \cref{item:BC for alpha} of \cref{lem:Bernstein condition for sync processes}, 
    $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[ \alpha_{t-1}(i)])$ conditioned on round $t-1$ satisfies $\qty(\frac{1}{n},s)$-Bernstein condition (this verifies the condition \ref{item:C2'}).

    \paragraph*{2-Choices.}
    We deal with two cases: $\alpha_{t-1}(i)\geq \gamma_{t-1}$ or not.
    First, suppose $\alpha_{t-1}(i)\geq \gamma_{t-1}$.
    We have $\gamma_{t-1}\leq \alpha_{t-1}(i)$ and $\alpha_{t-1}(i) \le (1+c_\alpha^{\uparrow})\alpha_0(i)$ if $ t-1 < \tau $.
    From \cref{lem:BC for SP} and \cref{item:BC for alpha} of \cref{lem:Bernstein condition for sync processes},
    $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[ \alpha_{t-1}(i)])$ conditioned on round $t-1$ satisfies  $\qty(\frac{1}{n},s)$-Bernstein condition.
    Hence, from \cref{item:dominated Bernstein condition} of \cref{lem:Bernstein condition}, the random variable
    $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i)-R)\leq \mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[ \alpha_{t-1}(i)])$ satisfies one-sided $\qty(\frac{1}{n},s)$-Bernstein condition.
    
  
  
  
  
    

    Second, consider the other case where $\alpha_{t-1}(i)\leq \gamma_{t-1}$.
    From \cref{lem:concentration of alpha difference for 2 choices} and \cref{item:Bernstein condition 2} of \cref{lem:Bernstein condition},
    the random variable $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i))$ satisfies one-sided $\qty(\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}}{n},\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\alpha_{t-1}(i)^2}{n})$-Bernstein condition.
    Hence, $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i)-R)\leq \mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i))$ satisfies one-sided $\qty(\frac{1}{n}, s)$-Bernstein condition from \cref{item:dominated Bernstein condition} of \cref{lem:Bernstein condition}.
    
    Hence, in any case, $\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(\alpha_t(i)-\alpha_{t-1}(i)-R)$ satisfies one-sided $\qty(\frac{1}{n}, s)$-Bernstein condition (this verifies the condition \ref{item:C2}).


    Applying \cref{item:positive drift} of \cref{lem:Freedman stopping time additive} for 
    $D=\frac{1}{n}$, $h=c^{\uparrow}_\alpha\alpha_0(i)$, and $T = \frac{C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:drift analysis for basic}(\ref{item:tauiup})}}}{ \alpha_0(i)}$ (then, $ z = h-R\cdot T = \varepsilon c^{\uparrow}_\alpha\alpha_0(i) $), we have
    \begin{align*}
    \Pr\qty[\tau\leq T]
    &=\Pr\qty[\tau_X^+\leq \min\{T,\tau\}]
    \le \exp\qty( -\Omega\qty(\frac{\alpha_0(i)^2}{ s T + \alpha_0(i)/n }) ),
    \end{align*}
    where $ \tau_X^+ = \inf\qty{ t\ge 0\colon X_t\ge X_0 + h } = \inf\{ t\ge 0\colon \alpha_t(i)\ge \alpha_0(i) + c^{\uparrow}_\alpha\alpha_0(i) \}= \tau^{\uparrow}_i$.
    Substituting \cref{eq:variance tauiup}, we obtain the claim.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{lem:taunormdown is large}
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we prove the claim for 3-Majority. The same proof works for 2-Choices. For each 0le s le T, let sigma^downarrow_s = inf\ tge s colon gamma_t le (1-c^downarrow_gamma) gamma_s \, sigma^uparrow_s = inf\t ge s colon gamma_t ge 2gamma_s\, and let E^(s) be the event that gamma_s ge gamma_0 and sigma^downarrow_s le min\T, sigma^uparrow_s\. Note that tau^downarrow_gamma = sigma^downarrow_0 and tau^uparrow_gamma = sigma^uparrow_0 (for c^uparrow_gamma=1). The key observation is that the partial process (alpha_t)_tge s is again a 3-Majority process and sigma_t^uparrow,sigma_t^downarrow can be seen as the stopping times of crefdef:stopping times for the partial process. Moreover, the event E^(s) depends only on the partial process (alpha_t)_tge s. Therefore, from crefitem:taunormdown of creflem:drift analysis for basic, we have Pr_(alpha_t)_tge sqty[ E^(s) ] &le Pr_(alpha_t)_tge sqty[ sigma_s^downarrow le min\T, sigma^uparrow_s\ middle| gamma_s ge gamma_0 ] \\ &le expqty( - Omegaqty( fracnsqrtgamma_0T)). If tau^downarrow_gamma le T occurs, then E^(s) occurs for some 0le s le T. For example, if sle tau^downarrow_gamma is the round such that gamma_s = max_0le t le tau^downarrow_gamma gamma_t, then E^(s) holds. Therefore, we have Prqty[ tau^downarrow_gamma le T ] &le Prqty[ bigvee_0le s le T E^(s) ] \\ &le sum_0le s le T Prqty[ E^(s)] \\ &le Texpqty( - Omegaqty( fracnsqrtgamma_0T )). Now, we prove the ``specifically'' part. For 3-Majority, substituting T=fracClog ngamma_0 yields the claim since fracnsqrtgamma_0T =fracngamma_0^1.5Clog n geq n^1/4sqrtC log n. For 2-Choices, substituting T=fracClog ngamma_0 yields the claim since fracnT+gamma_0^-1/2 = fracnfracClog ngamma_0+frac1sqrtgamma_0 geq fracnfracnClog n+fracsqrtnClog n geq fracClog n2.

\label{lem:taudeltaplus OST}
    Let $ i,j $ be distinct opinions.
    Consider the stopping times $ \tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_i,\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_j,\tau^{\downarrow}_i,\tau^{\downarrow}_j $ defined in \cref{def:stopping times}.
    Let $\tau\mathrel{\mathop:}= \min\{\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_i,\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_j,\tau^{\downarrow}_i,\tau^{\downarrow}_j\}$.
    Let $C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}= 1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(1-c^{\mathrm{weak}})}}$ be a positive constant defined in \cref{lem:two strong opinions}.

    \[
    \mathbb{E}[\tau]\leq \frac{\mathbb{E}\qty[\delta_\tau(i,j)^2]}{s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}},

    \end{cases*}.
    
    \end{align*}

Suppose $\tau>t-1$.
    First, we show that $\mathbf{Var}_{t-1}\geq s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}$ for 3-Majority and 2-Choices.
    Indeed, for 3-Majority, 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbf{Var}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]
        &\geq C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^3\frac{\alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(j)}{n} &&(\because \textrm{\cref{item:lower bound for variance} of \cref{lem:two strong opinions}}) \nonumber\\
        &\geq C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^3(1-c^{\downarrow}_\alpha)\frac{\alpha_{0}(i)+\alpha_{0}(j)}{n} &&(\because \tau^{\downarrow}_i,\tau^{\downarrow}_j>t-1) \nonumber\\
        
        &\geq s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}
    \end{align*}
    holds and for 2-Choices, 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbf{Var}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]
        &\geq C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^2\frac{\alpha_{t-1}(i)^2+\alpha_{t-1}(j)^2}{n} &&(\because \textrm{\cref{item:lower bound for variance} of \cref{lem:two strong opinions}}) \nonumber\\
        &\geq C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^2(1-c^{\downarrow}_\alpha)^2\frac{\alpha_{0}(i)^2+\alpha_{0}(j)^2}{n} &&(\because \tau^{\downarrow}_i,\tau^{\downarrow}_j>t-1) \nonumber\\
        
        &\geq s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}
    \end{align*}
    holds.
    Hence, for both models, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\delta_t^2]
        &=\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\delta_t]^2+\mathbf{Var}_{t-1}[\delta_t]\\
        &=\delta_{t-1}^2\qty(1+\alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(j)-\gamma_{t-1})^2+\mathbf{Var}_{t-1}[\delta_t]\\
        &\geq \delta_{t-1}^2\qty(1+\frac{1-2c^{\mathrm{weak}}}{1-c^{\mathrm{weak}}}\max\{\alpha_{t-1}(i),\alpha_{t-1}(j)\})^2+s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}} &&(\text{$\because$ \cref{item:lower bound for multipricative term} of \cref{lem:two strong opinions}})\\
        &\geq \delta_{t-1}^2+s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}.
    \end{align*}
    Let $X_t=s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}} \cdot t-\delta_t^2$
    and $Y_t=X_{t\wedge \tau}$.
    Then,
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[Y_t-Y_{t-1}]
    =\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[X_t-X_{t-1}]
    =\mathbf{1}_{\tau>t-1}\qty(s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}\cdot t-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\delta_t^2]-s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}\cdot (t-1)+\delta_{t-1}^2)
    \leq 0,
    \end{align*}
    i.e., $(Y_t)_{t\in \mathbb{N}_0}$ is a supermartingale.
    Hence, applying the optimal stopping theorem (\cref{thm:OST}),
    $\mathbb{E}[Y_\tau]\leq \mathbb{E}[Y_0]=-\delta_0^2\leq 0$.
    Furthermore, $\mathbb{E}[Y_\tau]=\mathbb{E}[X_\tau]=s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}\mathbb{E}[\tau]-\mathbb{E}[\delta_\tau^2]$ holds from definition.
    Thus, 
    \begin{align*}
        s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}\mathbb{E}[\tau]-\mathbb{E}[\delta_\tau^2]=\mathbb{E}[Y_\tau]\leq \mathbb{E}[Y_0]\leq 0
    \end{align*}
    holds and we obtain the claim.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{lem:gap amplification}.
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we prove for 3-Majority. The proof for 2-Choices can be obtained by the same way. We apply creflem:nazo lemma, where each Z_t in [k]^V is an opinion configuration, tau = min\tau^weak_i,tau^weak_j,tau^downarrow_gamma\ , varphi(Z_t) = sqrtncdot absdelta_t . From creflem:deltaupweak,lem:additive drift, for a sufficiently large constant C_0>0 and for T_0 = fracC_0max\alpha_0(i),alpha_0(j)\ , we have &Prqty[ minqty tau^+_delta,tau > T_0 ] le 1-Omega(1),\\ &Prqty[ minqty tau^uparrow_delta, tau > T_0 ] le expqty( -Omega(ngamma_0^2) ) + expqty( -Omega(ndelta_0^2) ) le expqty( -Omega(varphi(Z_0)^2) ). Here, note that gamma_0 = omega(sqrtlog n/n) and thus the term expqty( -Omega(ngamma_0^2) ) = n^-omega(1) is negligible. By definition of tau , for any t < tau , we have maxqtyalpha_t(i),alpha_t(j) ge (1-c^weak)gamma_0 . Therefore, crefeq:inequalities of nazolemma holds even if we replace T_0 by Tmathrelmathop:= fracC_0(1-c^weak)gamma_0 . Let c >0 be an arbitrary large constant (as considered in creflem:gap amplification). From creflem:nazo lemma for varepsilon = n^-10 , x_0 = c^+_delta (the constant of creflem:additive drift) and x^*=csqrtlog n , with probability 1-O(n^-10) , within O(Tcdot log n) rounds, we have either t= tau = min\tau^weak_i,tau^weak_j,tau^downarrow_gamma\ or varphi(Z_t) ge csqrtlog n , i.e., absdelta_t ge csqrtlog n / n . From creflem:taunormdown is large, the event t=tau^downarrow_gamma does not occur during the consecutive O(Tcdot log n) rounds with probability 1-O(n^-10) . Therefore, we obtain the claim.

For simplicity, we prove for 3-Majority.
  The proof for 2-Choices can be obtained by the same way.
  We apply \cref{lem:nazo lemma}, where each $ Z_t \in [k]^V $ is an opinion configuration,
  $ \tau = \min\{\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_i,\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_j,\tau^{\downarrow}_\gamma\} $, $ \varphi(Z_t) = \sqrt{n}\cdot \abs{\delta_t} $.
  From \cref{lem:deltaupweak,lem:additive drift}, for a sufficiently large constant $ C_0>0 $ and for $ T_0 = \frac{C_0}{\max\{\alpha_0(i),\alpha_0(j)\}} $, we have
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:inequalities of nazolemma}
    \begin{aligned}
    &\Pr\qty[ \min\qty{ \tau^{+}_\delta,\tau } > T_0 ] \le 1-\Omega(1),\\
    &\Pr\qty[ \min\qty{ \tau^{\uparrow}_\delta, \tau } > T_0 ] \le \exp\qty( -\Omega(n\gamma_0^2) ) + \exp\qty( -\Omega(n\delta_0^2) ) \le \exp\qty( -\Omega(\varphi(Z_0)^2) ).
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  Here, note that $ \gamma_0 = \omega(\sqrt{\log n/n}) $ and thus the term $ \exp\qty( -\Omega(n\gamma_0^2) ) = n^{-\omega(1)}$ is negligible.
  By definition of $ \tau $, for any $ t < \tau $, we have $ \max\qty{\alpha_t(i),\alpha_t(j)} \ge (1-c^{\mathrm{weak}})\gamma_0 $.
  Therefore, \cref{eq:inequalities of nazolemma} holds even if we replace $ T_0 $ by $ T\mathrel{\mathop:}= \frac{C_0}{(1-c^{\mathrm{weak}})\gamma_0} $.

  Let $ c >0$ be an arbitrary large constant (as considered in \cref{lem:gap amplification}).
  From \cref{lem:nazo lemma} for $ \varepsilon = n^{-10} $, $ x_0 = c^{+}_\delta $ (the constant of \cref{lem:additive drift}) and $ x^*=c\sqrt{\log n} $, with probability $ 1-O(n^{-10}) $,
  within $ O(T\cdot \log n) $ rounds, we have either $ t= \tau = \min\{\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_i,\tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_j,\tau^{\downarrow}_\gamma\}$ or $ \varphi(Z_t) \ge c\sqrt{\log n} $, i.e., $ \abs{\delta_t} \ge c\sqrt{\log n / n} $.
  From \cref{lem:taunormdown is large}, the event $ t=\tau^{\downarrow}_\gamma $ does not occur during the consecutive $ O(T\cdot \log n) $ rounds with probability $ 1-O(n^{-10}) $.
  Therefore, we obtain the claim.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{thm:consensus time large alphanorm}.
nodes.statement: Consider 3-Majority (the proof for 2-Choices is similar). Suppose that the initial configuration satisfies gamma_0 ge fracClog nsqrtn, where C>0 is a sufficiently large constant. Fix any two distinct opinions i,j . From creflem:taunormdown is large, we may assume that gamma_t =Omega(gamma_0) during the process. From creflem:gap amplification,lem:initial bias weak, either i or j becomes weak within O((log n)/gamma_0) rounds with probability 1-O(n^-10). Moreover, from creflem:weakvanish with probability 1-O(n^-10) , every weak opinion vanishes within O((log n)/gamma_0) rounds. Therefore, by the union bound over ine j , with probability 1-O(n^-8) , for any pair of distinct opinions, either i or j vanishes within O((log n)/gamma_0) rounds. This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{thm:growth of alphanorm}.
nodes.statement: Consider 3-Majority (the proof for 2-Choices is similar). Let C>0 be a sufficiently large constant. From creflem:taunormplus for x_gamma = Clog n / sqrtn, we have gamma_t ge Clog n/sqrtn with probability 1/2 within t=O(sqrtnlog n) rounds. Repeating this argument for O(log n) times, with high probability, we have gamma_T ge Clog n / sqrtn for some T=O(sqrtn(log n)^2).

nodes.statement: Random variables X_1,ldots,X_n are negatively associated if for every two disjoint index sets I,Jsubseteq [n], \[ Eqty[f(X_i,iin I)g(X_j,jin J)]leq Eqty[f(X_i,iin I)]Eqty[g(X_j,jin J)] \] for all functions f:R^Ito R and g:R^Jto R that are both non-decreasing.

\label{def:NA}
    Random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are \emph{negatively associated} if 
    for every two disjoint index sets $I,J\subseteq [n]$,
    \[
    \mathbb{E}\qty[f(X_i,i\in I)g(X_j,j\in J)]\leq \mathbb{E}\qty[f(X_i,i\in I)]\mathbb{E}\qty[g(X_j,j\in J)]

    for all functions $f:\mathbb{R}^I\to \mathbb{R}$ and $g:\mathbb{R}^J\to \mathbb{R}$
    that are both non-decreasing.

    To begin with, we show $\mathbf{Var}_{t-1}[\delta_t]\leq C_{\delta} s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}$ for $\tau>t-1$.
    Indeed, for 3-Majority, 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbf{Var}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]
        &\leq \frac{2(\alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(j))}{n} &&(\because \textrm{\cref{item:delta} of \cref{lem:basic inequality}})\\
        
        &\leq \frac{(1+c^{\uparrow}_\alpha)(\alpha_{0}(i)+\alpha_{0}(j))}{n} &&(\because \tau^{\uparrow}_i,\tau^{\uparrow}_j>t-1)\\
        &\leq 2(1+c^{\uparrow}_\alpha)\frac{\max\{\alpha_0(i),\alpha_0(j)\}}{n}\\
        &=C_{\delta} s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}
    \end{align*}
    holds, and for 2-Choices, 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbf{Var}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]
        &\leq \frac{(\alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(j))(\alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(j)+\gamma_{t-1})}{n} &&(\because \textrm{\cref{item:delta} of \cref{lem:basic inequality}})\\
        &\leq \frac{(\alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(j))\qty(\alpha_{t-1}(i)+\alpha_{t-1}(j)+\frac{\alpha_{t-1}(i)}{1-c^{\mathrm{weak}}})}{n}&&(\because \tau^{\mathrm{weak}}_i>t-1)\\
        &\leq \frac{(1+c^{\uparrow}_\alpha)^2(\alpha_{0}(i)+\alpha_{0}(j))\qty(\frac{2-c^{\mathrm{weak}}}{1-c^{\mathrm{weak}}}\alpha_{0}(i)+\alpha_{0}(j))}{n} &&(\because \tau^{\uparrow}_i,\tau^{\uparrow}_j>t-1)\\
        &\leq 2(1+c^{\uparrow}_\alpha)^2\frac{3-2c^{\mathrm{weak}}}{1-c^{\mathrm{weak}}} \cdot \frac{\max\{\alpha_0(i),\alpha_0(j)\}^2}{n}\\
        &=C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}.
    \end{align*}
    
    Next, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_{t}^2\mathbf{1}_{\delta_t^2> L}]
        =\int_{0}^1\Pr_{t-1}\qty[\delta_{t}^2\mathbf{1}_{\delta_t^2> L}>y]dy
        
        =\int_{0}^1\Pr_{t-1}\qty[\delta_{t}^2>(y\vee L)]dy
        =\int_{0}^1\Pr_{t-1}\qty[\abs{\delta_{t}}>\sqrt{y\vee L}]dy.
        
    \end{align*}
    We observe that
    $\abs{\delta_t}\leq \abs{\delta_t-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]}+\frac{\sqrt{y\vee L}}{2}$ holds for $\tau^{+}_\delta>t-1$, since
    $\abs{\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]}\leq 2\abs{\delta_{t-1}}\leq 2x_{\delta}$ and
    $\abs{\delta_t}\leq \abs{\delta_t-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]}+\abs{\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]}\leq \abs{\delta_t-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]}+2x_{\delta}\leq \abs{\delta_t-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]}+\frac{\sqrt{y\vee L}}{2}$ hold.
    Applying the Bernstein inequality (\cref{thm:Bernstein}) with $n\delta_t-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[n\delta_t]$, 
    \begin{align*}
        \Pr_{t-1}\qty[\abs{\delta_{t}}>\sqrt{y\vee L}]
        &\leq \Pr_{t-1}\qty[\abs{\delta_{t}-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]}>\frac{\sqrt{y\vee L}}{2}]\\
        &\leq \Pr_{t-1}\qty[\abs{n\delta_{t}-\mathbb{E}_{t-1}\qty[n\delta_t]}>\frac{n\sqrt{\max\{y\vee L\}}}{2}]\\
        &\leq 2\exp\qty(-\frac{(y\vee L)n^2/4}{\mathbf{Var}_{t-1}[n\delta_t]+\sqrt{\max\{y\vee L\}}n/6})
        && (\because \textrm{\cref{thm:Bernstein}})\\
        &\leq 2\exp\qty(-\frac{3n(y\vee L)/2}{6nC_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}+\sqrt{y\vee L}})
        && (\because \mathbf{Var}_{t-1}\qty[\delta_t]\leq C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}})\\
        &\leq 2\exp\qty(-\frac{3}{4}n\sqrt{y\vee L})
        +2\exp\qty(-\frac{y\vee L}{8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}})
    \end{align*}
    holds for $\tau>t-1$.
    
    By integrating each term, we obtain
    \begin{align*}
    &\int_0^1\exp\qty(-\frac{3}{4}n\sqrt{y\vee L})dy\\
    &=L\exp\qty(-\frac{3}{4}n\sqrt{L})+\int_L^1\exp\qty(-\frac{3}{4}n\sqrt{y})dy\\
    &\leq L\exp\qty(-\frac{3}{4}n\sqrt{L})+2\frac{(3/4)n\sqrt{L}+1}{(3/4)^2n^2}\exp\qty(-\frac{3}{4}n\sqrt{L})\\
    &\leq 2L\exp\qty(-\frac{3}{4}n\sqrt{L}) &&(\because L=16x_{\delta}^2\geq 16/n^2)
    \end{align*}
    and
    \begin{align*}
        \int_0^1\exp\qty(-\frac{\max\{L,y\}}{8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}})dy
        &=L\exp\qty(-\frac{L}{8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}})+\int_L^1\exp\qty(-\frac{y}{8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}})dy\\
        &\leq L\exp\qty(-\frac{L}{8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}})+8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}\exp\qty(-\frac{L}{8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}})\\
        &\leq 2L\exp\qty(-\frac{L}{8C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}}). &&(\because C_{\delta}\leq 2x_{\delta}^2/s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}})
        
    \end{align*}
    Now, we claim $\frac{x_{\delta}^2}{s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}}\leq n^4$ holds for both models and for a sufficiently large $n$.
    For 3-Majority, $\frac{x_{\delta}^2}{s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}}\leq \frac{n}{C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^3(1-c^{\downarrow}_\alpha)\max\{\alpha_0(i),\alpha_0(j)\}}\leq \frac{n^2}{C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^3(1-c^{\downarrow}_\alpha)}$.
    Similarly, for 2-Choices,
    $\frac{x_{\delta}^2}{s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}}\leq \frac{n}{C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^2(1-c^{\downarrow}_\alpha)^2\max\{\alpha_0(i),\alpha_0(j)\}^2}\leq \frac{n^3}{C_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:two strong opinions}}}^2(1-c^{\downarrow}_\alpha)^2}$.
    Consequently, for $\tau>t-1$, 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\delta_{t}^2\mathbf{1}_{\delta_t^2> L}]
        &\leq 2s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}\qty(\underbrace{\frac{16x_{\delta}^2}{s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}}}_{\leq 16n^{4}}\exp\qty(-3\underbrace{nx_{\delta}}_{\geq 2 \log n})
        +\underbrace{\frac{16x_{\delta}^2}{s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}}\exp\qty(-\frac{2x_{\delta}^2}{C_{\delta}s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}})}_{\leq 16/100})\\
        &\leq 32s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}\qty(n^{-2}+\frac{1}{100}) \\
        &\leq s_{\mbox{\tiny\ref{lem:taudeltaplus OST}}}/2
    \end{align*}
    holds for a sufficiently large $n$ and that concludes the claim.

        &=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n^2}\Pr_{t-1}\qty[A_t(i)^2\geq \ell \textrm{ and } A_{t}(i)\geq 4\mathrm{e} A_{t-1}(i)]\\

    \end{align*}

nodes.statement: We divide time into phases each consists of consecutive rounds of several length. Formally, the phase s begins at round tau(s) and ends at round tau(s+1) , where tau(s) = 0 & for s=0,\\ infqty t ge tau(s-1) colon &&&tge tau(s-1)+ T or \\ &&&tge tau or\\ &&&varphi(Z_t) ge maxqty x_0, (1+c_varphi^uparrow)varphiqty(Z_tau(s-1)) & for sge 1. We say that the phase s is good if it ends due to either the second or third condition being satisfied, i.e., tau(s) ge tau or varphi(Z_tau(s)) ge maxqty x_0, (1+c_varphi^uparrow)varphiqty(Z_tau(s-1)). Otherwise, the phase s is bad. For example, if the phase s ends with the condition tgetau , then tau(s+c) = tau(s) for all cinN_0 (the length of a phase can be zero); thus, all subsequent phases are good. We shall count the number of consecutive good phases starting from round 0 . By the first assumption of creflem:nazo lemma, for any z in Omega , conditioned on Z_0 = z , the phase 0 is good with probability C_1 ; then either tau(1)ge tau or varphi(Z_tau(1)) ge x_0 holds. Again, by the second assumption (and since (Z_t) is a Markov chain), conditioned on the event that the phase 0 is good, the phase 1 is good with probability 1-exp(-C_2 x_0^2) ; then either tau(2) ge tau or varphi(Z_tau(2)) ge (1 + c_varphi^uparrow)x_0 holds. By repeating this argument, conditioned on the event that the phases 0,dots,s-1 are good (in which case either tau(s-1) ge tau or varphi(Z_tau(s-1)) ge (1+c_varphi^uparrow)^s-1x_0 ), we have that the phase s is good with probability 1-exp(-C_2 (1+c_varphi^uparrow)^2s-2cdot x_0^2) . Let S be the number of consecutive good phases starting at round 0 . Note that S can be infty when a phase ends with the condition tge tau . For the target value x^* , let KinN be the minimum integer such that x_0 cdot (1+c_varphi^uparrow)^K ge x^* . Note that S>K implies that either tge tau or varphi(Z_t) ge x_0 cdot (1+c_varphi^uparrow)^K ge x^* for the time round t soon after the K+1 consecutive success phases, meaning that varphi(Z_t) reaches the target value x^* . Throughout the proof, we assume that the big-O notation hides factors depending on C_1, C_2,x_0 and c_varphi^uparrow . For any ell ge 0 and any Z_0inOmega , we have Prqty[ S > ell ] &= Prqty[ phases 0,dots,ell are good ] \\ &ge C_1 prod_s in [ell] qty( 1-exp(-C_2 (1+c_varphi^uparrow)^2s-2cdot x_0^2) ) \\ &ge C_1 prod_s in [ell] (1-p^s) & & for some p <1\\ &ge C_1cdot prod_sin[ell] expqty( -fracp^s1-p^s ) & & (because1-x ge e^-fracx1-x for all xin[0,1)) \\ &ge C_1cdot expqty(-fracp1-psum_sge 0 p^s) \\ &ge C_1cdot expqty(-fracp(1-p)^2) \\ &=Omega(1). Note that the inequality above holds regardless of the initial state Z_0 . Consider the sequence (Z_t)_tge 0 . Let the number of consecutive successful phases be denoted sequentially as S^(0),S^(1),dots. We stop the sequence (Z_t) when the number of consecutive good phases exceeds K . Therefore, the number of phases during this process is at most S^(0) + S^(1) + dots + S^(U) , where U in N is the smallest integer such that S^(U) > K (here, we set S^(U)=K+1 ). Since each S^(i) satisfies Pr[S^(i) > K] =Omega(1), we have U= O(log(1/varepsilon)) with probability 1-varepsilon (over randomness of (Z_t)). We obtain an upper tail of S^(0) + dots + S^(U-1) . If Pr[S^(i) > K] = 1 , then U=1 and we have S^(0) = K+1. If not, the marginal distribution of each S^(i) for i<U is the distribution of S conditioned on Sle K. Moreover, for any ell le K, Prqty[ S = ell \;middlevert\; Sle K] &le fracPrqty[S=ell]Prqty[Sle K] \\ &le O(1)cdot Prqty[ S=ell \;middlevert\; Sge ell ] \\ &=Prqty[phase ell is bad \;middlevert\; phases 0,dots,ell-1 are good] \\ &le exp(-C_2 (1+c_varphi^uparrow)^2ell-2cdot x_0^2) & if ellge 1 \\ 1-C_1 & if ell=0 \\ &le p^ell. & & for some p <1 In particular, Eqty[S \;middlevert\; S<infty] le O(1) . We divide time into phases each consists of consecutive rounds of several length.
    Formally, the phase $ s $ begins at round $ \tau(s) $ and ends at round $ \tau(s+1) $, where
    \begin{align*} 
        \tau(s)  = 
            \begin{cases}
                0	& \text{for $s=0$},\\
                \inf\qty{ t \ge \tau(s-1) \colon 
                \begin{aligned}
                &&&t\ge \tau(s-1)+ T  \text{ or} \\
                &&&t\ge \tau  \text{ or}\\
                &&&\varphi(Z_t) \ge \max\qty{  x_0, (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})\varphi\qty(Z_{\tau(s-1)}) }
                \end{aligned}
                } & \text{for $s\ge 1$}.
            \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    We say that the phase $ s $ is \emph{good} if it ends
    due to either the second or third condition being satisfied, i.e.,
    $ \tau(s) \ge \tau $ or $ \varphi(Z_{\tau(s)}) \ge \max\qty{  x_0, (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})\varphi\qty(Z_{\tau(s-1)})}$.
    Otherwise, the phase $ s $ is \emph{bad}.
    For example, if the phase $ s $ ends with the condition $ t\ge\tau $, then $ \tau(s+c) = \tau(s)$ for all $ c\in\mathbb{N}_0 $ (the length of a phase can be zero); thus, all subsequent phases are good.


    We shall count the number of consecutive good phases starting from round $ 0 $.
    By the first assumption of \cref{lem:nazo lemma}, for any $ z \in \Omega $, conditioned on $ Z_0 = z $,
    the phase $ 0 $ is good with probability $ C_1 $; then either $ \tau(1)\ge \tau $ or $ \varphi(Z_{\tau(1)}) \ge x_0$ holds.
    Again, by the second assumption (and since $ (Z_t) $ is a Markov chain), conditioned on the event that the phase $ 0 $ is good, the phase $ 1 $ is good with probability $ 1-\exp(-C_2 x_0^2) $; then either $ \tau(2) \ge \tau $ or $ \varphi(Z_{\tau(2)}) \ge (1 + c_\varphi^{\uparrow})x_0$ holds.
    By repeating this argument, conditioned on the event that the phases $0,\dots,s-1$ are good (in which case either $ \tau(s-1) \ge \tau $ or $ \varphi(Z_{\tau(s-1)}) \ge (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})^{s-1}x_0 $), we have that the phase $ s $ is good with probability $ 1-\exp(-C_2 (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})^{2s-2}\cdot x_0^2) $.
    Let $ S $ be the number of consecutive good phases starting at round $ 0 $.
    Note that $ S $ can be $ \infty $ when a phase ends with the condition $ t\ge \tau $.
    For the target value $ x^* $, let $ K\in\mathbb{N} $ be the minimum integer such that $ x_0 \cdot (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})^K \ge x^* $.
    Note that $ S>K $ implies that either $ t\ge \tau $ or $ \varphi(Z_t) \ge x_0 \cdot (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})^K \ge x^*$ for the time round $ t $ soon after the $ K+1 $ consecutive success phases, meaning that $ \varphi(Z_t) $ reaches the target value $ x^* $.

    Throughout the proof, we assume that the big-O notation hides factors depending on $C_1, C_2,x_0 $ and $ c_\varphi^{\uparrow} $.
    For any $ \ell \ge 0 $ and any $ Z_0\in\Omega $, we have
    \begin{align*} 
        \Pr\qty[ S > \ell ] &= \Pr\qty[ \text{phases $0,\dots,\ell$ are good} ]  \\
        &\ge C_1 \prod_{s \in [\ell]} \qty( 1-\exp(-C_2 (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})^{2s-2}\cdot x_0^2) ) \\
        &\ge C_1 \prod_{s \in [\ell]} (1-p^s) & & \text{for some $ p <1$}\\
        &\ge C_1\cdot \prod_{s\in[\ell]} \exp\qty( -\frac{p^s}{1-p^s} ) & & (\because\text{$1-x \ge \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{x}{1-x}}$ for all $x\in[0,1)$}) \\
        &\ge C_1\cdot \exp\qty(-\frac{p}{1-p}\sum_{s\ge 0} p^s) \\
        &\ge C_1\cdot \exp\qty(-\frac{p}{(1-p)^2}) \\
        &=\Omega(1).
    \end{align*}
    Note that the inequality above holds regardless of the initial state $ Z_0 $.

    Consider the sequence $ (Z_t)_{t\ge 0} $.
    Let the number of consecutive successful phases be denoted sequentially as $S^{(0)},S^{(1)},\dots$.
    We stop the sequence $ (Z_t) $ when the number of consecutive good phases exceeds $ K $.
    Therefore, the number of phases during this process is at most $ S^{(0)} + S^{(1)} + \dots + S^{(U)} $,
        where $ U \in \mathbb{N} $ is the smallest integer such that $ S^{(U)} > K $ (here, we set $ S^{(U)}=K+1 $).
    Since each $ S^{(i)} $ satisfies $ \Pr[S^{(i)} > K] =\Omega(1)$, we have $ U= O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) $ with probability $ 1-\varepsilon $ (over randomness of $ (Z_t)$).

    We obtain an upper tail of $ S^{(0)} + \dots + S^{(U-1)} $.
    If $ \Pr[S^{(i)} > K] = 1 $, then $ U=1 $ and we have $ S^{(0)} = K+1$.
    If not, the marginal distribution of each $ S^{(i)} $ for $ i<U $ is the distribution of $ S $ conditioned on $ S\le K$.
    Moreover, for any $ \ell \le K$,
    \begin{align*}
        \Pr\qty[ S = \ell \;\middle\vert\; S\le K] &\le \frac{\Pr\qty[S=\ell]}{\Pr\qty[S\le K]} \\
        &\le O(1)\cdot \Pr\qty[ S=\ell \;\middle\vert\; S\ge \ell ] \\
        &=\Pr\qty[\text{phase $\ell$ is bad} \;\middle\vert\; \text{phases $0,\dots,\ell-1$ are good}] \\
        &\le \begin{cases}
            \exp(-C_2 (1+c_\varphi^{\uparrow})^{2\ell-2}\cdot x_0^2) & \text{if $\ell\ge 1$} \\
            1-C_1 & \text{if $\ell=0$}
        \end{cases} \\
        &\le p^\ell.  & & \text{for some $ p <1$}
    \end{align*}
    In particular, $ \mathbb{E}\qty[S \;\middle\vert\; S<\infty] \le O(1) $.
    Therefore, conditioned on $ U $, for a sufficiently large constant $ C'>0 $,
    from \cref{lem:concentration exponentially decay} (for $ \mu = O(U),m=U,\gamma = C'\log(1/\varepsilon)/\mu $),
    we have
    \begin{align*}
        \Pr\qty[ S^{(0)} + \dots +S^{(U-1)} \ge C'\log(1/\varepsilon) ] \le \varepsilon^{-\Omega(1)}.
    \end{align*}

    Therefore, for any $ \varepsilon>0 $, we have $ S^{(0)} + \dots + S^{(U)} = O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) + K = O(\log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(x^*/x_0)) $ with probability $ 1-\varepsilon $.

Therefore, for any varepsilon>0 , we have S^(0) + dots + S^(U) = O(log(1/varepsilon)) + K = O(log(1/varepsilon) + log(x^*/x_0)) with probability 1-varepsilon .
